title: Is Malaysia working?
subtitle: Unemployment & the labour force, 2010–2026
question: What is Malaysia's unemployment rate?
answer: Malaysia's unemployment rate is 3.0% as of early 2026, near its lowest in over a decade, with a record 70.9% of working-age adults in the labour force. It spiked to 4.6% in 2021 during COVID before recovering.

source.notes: Annual figures are averages of monthly Labour Force Survey data. Unemployment rate = unemployed persons as a share of the labour force. Participation rate = share of working-age adults in the labour force. 2026 figures reflect data to April 2026.

headline.label: Participation rate
headline.sub: record high · adults in the workforce

trend.title: The COVID spike, and the recovery
trend.note: Unemployment rate (annual average), 2010–2025. It jumped during the pandemic, then fell back toward pre-COVID lows.

participation.title: More Malaysians are working than ever
participation.note: Labour force participation rate (share of working-age adults in the workforce), 2010–2025, now at record highs, led by rising women's participation.

takeaways: Unemployment spiked to **4.6% in 2021**, the worst in decades, as COVID hit, then fell steadily back to **3.0%**, near pre-pandemic lows.
A record **70.9%** of working-age Malaysians are now in the labour force, up from about 64% in 2010, driven largely by more women working.
Around **512,000** Malaysians were unemployed in early 2026, out of a **17.3 million**-strong labour force.
A 'low' 3% headline doesn't capture underemployment or people outside the labour force, it counts only those actively seeking work.

faq.a: Malaysia's unemployment rate was 3.0% as of early 2026, according to the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), near its lowest in over a decade.

faq.q: What was Malaysia's unemployment rate during COVID?
faq.a: It rose sharply during the pandemic, peaking at about 4.6% in 2021 (annual average), before recovering toward 3%.

faq.q: What is Malaysia's labour force participation rate?
faq.a: A record 70.9% of working-age adults were in the labour force in early 2026 (DOSM), up from around 64% in 2010.
